The test vane had 44 rows of cooling holes with diameters ranging from 0.33 to 0.84 mm and an area-averaged diameter of about 0.5 mm.
The cascade tunnel had 10 vanes with a span of 10.16 cm, but only 3 of the central vanes were cooled.
Cold air was used for both the primary and coolant flows, with the temperatures being very nearly equal.
The cascade tests covered a range of exit velocity ratios from 0.6 to 0.95 and coolant flow rates up to 7.5% of the primary flow.
The thermodynamic loss coefficient of the cooled vane was about 3 times higher than the uncooled vane at the design exit velocity ratio of 0.8.
The higher losses of the cooled vane were attributed to pressure losses and maldistribution of the coolant flow in the internal cooling passages.
The primary flow decreased by about 1% for every 1% increase in coolant flow.
The Zweifel loading coefficient for the uncooled vane was 0.789, indicating moderately high loading.
The flow angle of the uncooled vanes was about 1.5 degrees higher than the three-cooled-vane configuration at the design exit velocity ratio.
The single-cooled-vane configuration showed some differences in the repeating pattern of exit flow angle and mass flow compared to the three-cooled-vane configuration.
Using only one cooled vane may be satisfactory for comparing losses of vanes with similar cooling designs, but three cooled vanes better simulates the flow field of 10 cooled vanes.
The cascade tests provided a convenient and inexpensive method of determining the relative performance of different types of cooled turbine vanes.
The test vane was representative of an advanced high-temperature-core engine application, with an internal liner to distribute the cooling flow.
The principal measurements were cross-channel surveys of exit total pressure, static pressure, and flow angle.
The aftermix performance parameters were calculated from the exit survey measurements.
